lesson.title: The Layer That Finds the Right Program
lesson.summary: The transport layer turns host-to-host delivery from the network layer into process-to-process delivery, using port numbers to route data to the correct application and, depending on the protocol chosen, adding reliability, ordering, and flow control.
lesson.body:
The OSI reference model places the transport layer at layer 4, sitting between the network layer below (which only promises to get a packet from one host to another host) and the session, presentation, and application layers above. The TCP IP model keeps this same layer but flattens everything above it into a single application layer. Either way, the transport layer solves a problem the network layer cannot: a computer runs dozens of programs at once, and a packet addressed to an IP address alone does not say which program on that machine should receive it.

The transport layer solves this with port numbers. Every TCP or UDP segment carries a source port and a destination port in its header, and the operating system uses this pair, combined with the IP addresses, to demultiplex incoming data to the correct socket and therefore the correct process. A web server listening on port 443 can be reached by thousands of different client connections at once, each identified by a different source port and source IP, and the operating system's transport layer sorts every incoming segment into the right bucket without the application ever having to think about routing.

Beyond addressing, the transport layer is where the two dominant service models of the internet live: TCP and UDP. TCP breaks application data into segments, numbers them, and rebuilds an ordered, reliable byte stream at the far end, adding flow control so a fast sender cannot overrun a slow receiver, and congestion control so competing flows share a network path reasonably. UDP does almost none of this. It hands each chunk of data to the network layer as an independent datagram and lets the application layer decide whether ordering or retransmission matters. Both protocols are covered in more depth once connection oriented and connectionless service models are introduced, but the key point here is that the choice between them is made at the transport layer, per connection, by the application that opens the socket.

A concrete example makes the layering clear. When a browser loads a page over HTTPS, it first asks DNS to resolve a hostname to an IP address, then opens a TCP connection to that IP address on port 443. The TCP handshake, sequence numbers, and acknowledgments all happen at the transport layer, invisible to the HTTP request and response text that rides on top of it. If the user opens ten browser tabs to the same server, the operating system assigns ten different ephemeral source ports, so ten independent TCP connections coexist over the same physical link without ever being confused for one another.

This is also where the TCP IP model's four layer view and the OSI model's seven layer view start to diverge in a way worth naming honestly. OSI reserves layers 5 through 7 for session, presentation, and application concerns, while TCP IP folds all of that into one application layer that simply assumes those functions happen somewhere above the socket interface. The transport layer is the last layer both models agree on in the same place, which is one reason textbooks and interviewers alike treat it as the seam of the stack: everything below it is about getting bytes somewhere, and everything above it is about what those bytes mean.
